https://hungarytoday.hu/national-museum-.text: National Museum Explores 250 Years of Hungarian–American Connections The Hungarian National Museum officially opened its new exhibition, The American Dream: Hungarians in the United States, 1776–2026 , commemorating the 250th anniversary of American independence and celebrating the enduring relationship between Hungary and the United States. Through stories of migration, achievement, and shared democratic values, the exhibition explores how generations of Hungarians helped shape American society while maintaining strong cultural ties to their homeland, underscoring the themes of freedom, opportunity, and perseverance that have connected the two nations for nearly two and a half centuries. Part of the exhibition. Photo: MTI/Bodnár Boglárka Dr. Gábor Zsigmond, Director General of the Hungarian National Museum, emphasized in his speech that few anniversaries in world history are both a national celebration and a milestone in our shared human history, however, the 250th anniversary of the independence of the United States is one such occasion. Mementos of the American “Kossuth fever”. Books on Kossuth and the Hungarian struggle for independence. Photo: Hungary Today Today, we commemorate not only the birth of a nation, but also an idea that has inspired millions of people across generations: the belief that freedom, personal responsibility, perseverance and opportunity can come together to create a new life,” he said. Dr. Gábor Zsigmond, Director General of the Hungarian National Museum, at the event. Photo: Hungary Today The director explained that this exhibition and celebration carries particular significance. “Our institute serves as the guardian of Hungary’s historical memory. For nearly 225 years, we have collected, preserved, researched, and interpreted the material and intellectual heritage that has shaped the Hungarian nation, and that heritage also includes the lives of Hungarians beyond the borders.” Iroquois-style Native American footwear. Kossuth received it from an Iroquois woman during his American tour. Photo: Hungary Today Caroline Savage, Chargé d’Affaires of the U.S. Embassy in Hungary pointed out that the event celebrates not only the 250th anniversary of the independence, but also an enduring friendship and mutual respect between the United States and Hungary. Caroline Savage, Chargé d’Affaires of the U.S. Embassy in Hungary . Photo: Hungary Today She emphasized that the American dream has never belonged to just one person: “It has been shaped by the talents, perseverance, and cultural heritage of millions of people, all of whom have contributed to the development of the United States. Hungarians have been an important part of this story from the earliest days of our nation,” she pointed out. The iconic Hungarian flag with a hole in the center became the defining symbol of the 1956 Revolution. Photo: Hungary Today Historians and curators of the exhibition Dr. Klára Radnoti and Dr. Angelika Orgona stated that the exhibition has three key themes: the desire for freedom, prosperity and success. Sándor Márai’s Remington typewriter and Katalin Karády’s cigarette case. Photo: Hungary Today These form the main sections, each with their own stories, through which they aimed to present the historical and cultural ties between Hungary and the United States. Artifacts celebrating Hungarian contributions to Hollywood: a Terminator sculpture by Zoltán Rónaszéki, Tony Curtis’s director’s chair, Zsa Zsa Gábor’s cocktail dress, and an Oscar statuette displayed in the background. Photo: Hungary Today. No single exhibition can offer a complete account of the history of Hungarian emigration and the diaspora. But we have tried to convey something of their diversity, the curators said. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Damage in Myla village after a Russian attack on an ammunition warehouse. The detonation affected the residential areas nearby. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Ukraine ‘Everything’s smashed to bits’: Ukrainians turn anger on those storing weapons near their villages As Russia hits another ammunition warehouse, killing at least 38, locals put blame on poorly placed depots Dan Sabbagh in Myla, Kyiv region. Photography by Julia Kochetova Mon 31 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I t is a day and a half since a Russian jet-powered drone smashed into an ammunition dump in Myla , a village 15 miles outside central Kyiv. Volodymyr, 61, a security guard, leads visitors from his family’s badly damaged home, its roof blown off, back windows shattered, through the garden towards the impact site 300 metres away. The garden, like so many in Ukraine’s villages and suburbs, is a sizeable allotment. But today the greenhouse is shattered, a vegetable patch is blackened and crisp underfoot. Several metres of grapevine have been destroyed. Even so, Volodymyr finds two surviving bunches to hand to the Guardian. View image in fullscreen Inside the damaged house in Myla village, Kyiv region. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian It is a remarkable moment of generosity, though his family now has no electricity and no water after Thursday night’s extended bombing. The death toll rose by one on Sunday, to 38, and four more people are still missing in an episode that has swiftly raised questions about why ammunition was stored so close to people’s homes. In the yard before the garden, Vira, 65, knows who is at fault. “Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” she says. She and her son Serhii hid for hours in a small bunker by the side of the house waiting out what witnesses said were 30 or 50 explosions that went on for about six hours after the initial strike at 8pm. Map showing where Myla is in relation to Bucha and Kyiv Serhii says they had no idea ammunition was stored in their village. “I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there.” Now the family is presented with a cleanup that will be costly and difficult while starting with next to nothing. He is charging his phone from a car battery via a converter. It is all the power they have. A missile shell from a Grad rocket launcher was found on their property once the explosions subsided, Serhii adds, as well as “several mines and cluster munitions”. They have been removed by the cleanup team, although a burnt-out box of bullets, freshly discovered in another part of the semi-collapsed ceiling, has not and sits by the front door awaiting a further collection. View image in fullscreen Volodymyr shows his working place where he was during the attack. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Volodymyr’s tour continues out back. A grass line, effectively a track, has been marked out through the wood beyond the garden, between blackened patches where fires burned. There is smouldering, even flames in places, more bullets and boxes of bullets, then, on the right, unmistakably, a detonated anti-tank mine. Finally, the woods open out, revealing a warehouse site, large parts of which are bombed out, an open area of destruction. A sulphurous smell endures, and periodically explosions can be heard, though they may be controlled detonations. Clear-up work by the emergency services is in the process of being halted at lunchtime because there is another drone threat above. View image in fullscreen Rescue services are still working on the site. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Volodymyr was on guard duty at a lumber yard close to the ammunition store on the night of the bombing. He survived the initial strike unscathed, and headed back home promptly, but feels a guard’s need to return. “I’ve been coming back and forth for two days to see these ashes,” he says. Thirty of the dead were from a care home close to the ammunition store, the location of which is now subject of a criminal inquiry by Ukraine’s intelligence service. But it is not the first attack of its kind in recent weeks. There have been other Russian bombings of poorly placed ammunition dumps, as Moscow aggressively targets warehouse sites at a time when Ukraine is doing similar. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The fact this has happened recently in Ukraine is not lost on Liudmyla, whose adult daughter was in the house a couple of doors down when the Shahed drone hit. The home is also heavily damaged, windows facing the warehouse blown in, and Liudmyla recalls that a similar incident happened in early July, on the edge of Kyiv. View image in fullscreen Liudmyla near her damaged house. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian “Look at what’s going on here. Everything’s smashed to bits right here. Vyshneve [the scene of the previous incident, nine miles south-east] wasn’t enough for them, and there was more somewhere else too. No, they’ve dumped all this right by people’s vegetable gardens, right on their doorsteps,” she says, warning that munitions are still strewn around, not yet cleared up. Nine people were killed after a munitions store was hit at Vyshneve, and 280 homes damaged. Two people have been detained on suspicion of allowing weapons to be stored in an inappropriate place after the episode, but as the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Saturday, similar has happened again. It is a dismal repetition at a time when Kyiv is already coming under increased attack from Moscow, the harm to civilians from attacks on food stores and logistics warehouses increasing. When Liudmyla is pressed to say who is at fault for the deaths and destruction at Myla, she offers a double answer. “Putin! Who else? And those who set up the depot here.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Kountz 1948-2026 September 21, 2026 Trending STRUTHERS -- Daniel L. "Danny" Kountz, 78, passed away peacefully Monday morning, Aug. 31, 2026, with his family by his side. Born Aug. 14, 1948, in Youngstown, Dan was the son of George and Frances Pascarella Kountz. Throughout his life, he was a man of service, hard work, and quiet dedication to the people and things that mattered most to him. Dan proudly served his country in the United States Marine Corps during the Vietnam War. His military service was an important part of his life and a source of lasting pride. He earned the National Defense Medal, Combat Action Ribbon, Rifle Sharpshooter Badge, Good Conduct Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, and Vietnam Campaign Medal. His courage and commitment to his country will always be remembered and honored. Following his military service, Dan continued a life of service and hard work. He worked as an EMT, helping others during moments when they needed it most, and later worked for the Mahoning County Engineer's Office. He took pride in his work and the responsibility of doing a job well. Away from work, Dan found happiness in the things he could build, repair and make his own. He enjoyed woodworking, working on motorcycles, and riding his Harley. Whether he was in the garage with a project or out on the open road, these were the moments that reflected his independence, his skill, and his love of life. Above all, Dan was a father, grandfather, brother, uncle and friend whose presence will be deeply missed. His family will remember his profound presence, the things he taught them, the gifts he made for them, the time they spent together and the ordinary moments that now mean so much. The love he gave will forever remain a part of their lives. He had a way of making his words count, and those who knew him understood the meaning behind even his simple remarks. "Dan's gotta go." It became his unmistakable way of saying goodbye -- a phrase that could bring a smile to the room and one his family will forever hear in his voice. Dan will be lovingly remembered by his daughter, Lee (Erika) Kountz; his son, Dylan (Breanna) Kountz; his grandson, Ryker; and several loving nieces and nephews. In addition to his parents, he was preceded in death by his sister, Jeannette Kountz; and his brother, John Kountz. Family and friends may pay their respects as they gather for a Celebration of Life from 1:30 to 5:30 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, at The Stonewall Lodge, 10250 Springfield Road, Poland, OH 44514. Dan's dedicated service to his country will be recognized with full military honors. Family and friends are encouraged to offer prayers for the family and share memories of Dan through the Book of Memories at www.rossifunerals.com. Dan will be remembered by how he served, worked, loved and lived. He leaves behind a legacy of strength, devotion and memories that will be carried forward by those who loved him. Semper Fi. Arrangements have been entrusted to the professional care of the Rossi Brothers and Lellio Funeral Home, 4442 South Ave., Boardman. (special notice) Starting at /week. Subscribe Today

https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymy.text: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for approving the sale of Patriot interceptors but urged Washington to fast-track the delivery of the defensive missiles. Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision” by the U.S. to approve the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors to counter Russian ballistic missiles — but said the years-long wait to deliver them was too long for Ukraine's urgent needs. “It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy wrote in a Facebook post on Friday night. Advertisement Advertisement “We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added. Patriot interceptors are crucial for Ukraine to defend itself against Russia’s ballistic missiles, amid fears that Moscow will ramp up its attacks on energy facilities to bring winter blackouts in Ukraine. In the Facebook post, Zelenskyy said an immediate delivery of Patriot interceptors would allow Ukraine to defend its energy infrastructure during the winter season. “Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS” would be the right approach, Zelenskyy said. The U.S. decision to sell the interceptors signals a thaw in relations between the White House and Kyiv after tensions escalated in recent months . However, the White House said that it won't pay for the Patriot interceptors. "The estimated total cost is $2.1 billion funded entirely by partners and allies," a statement from the State Department said . Advertisement Advertisement
